common_name: Algerian Winter Iris (Winter Iris, Lazy Man's Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, poor, alkaline, sharply drained soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun; the straight species is seed-variable in flower color and vigor compared with named clones, but shares the same intolerance of rich soil and disturbance.

directions: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, poor, alkaline, sharply drained soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun, and resist the urge to enrich the soil or divide often. The straight species, native to Algeria, Tunisia, Greece, and Turkey, produces sweetly fragrant violet-blue flowers with yellow-veined falls through the darkest weeks of winter, when almost nothing else is in bloom, but shows more variable flower color and vigor from seedling to seedling than named clones such as 'Mary Barnard' or 'Walter Butt'. Like those selections, it flowers best when starved, crowded, and left completely undisturbed for several years, so avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, or frequent division.

common_name: Alba Algerian Winter Iris (White-Flowered Winter Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, poor, sharply drained, alkaline soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun; avoid rich soil or frequent division, which delay bloom.

directions: 'Alba' is a pure white-flowered selection of the Algerian winter iris, opening its blooms above narrow, grass-like evergreen leaves from midwinter into early spring in the same lean, dry, alkaline soil the species demands. Plant divisions in late summer to fall at the base of a warm, sunny wall, and avoid rich or regularly watered soil, which encourages lush foliage at the expense of flowers. Like other named forms of this species, it dislikes disturbance and can sulk for a season or two after transplanting before resuming full bloom.

common_name: Marondera Algerian Winter Iris (Zimbabwe-Collected Winter Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun, keeping the site dry and undisturbed to encourage repeat winter flowering.

directions: 'Marondera' was collected near Marondera, Zimbabwe, and stands out among named Algerian winter iris selections for its unusually large, pale lavender-blue flowers with fine white and gold veining, produced more freely than many seed-grown plants of the species. Plant divisions in late summer to fall in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil at the base of a warm, south-facing wall in full sun, and keep the site dry and undisturbed to encourage repeat flowering through the winter months. As with other unguicularis selections, rich soil or excess moisture will produce vigorous leaves rather than the flowers this iris is grown for.

planting.note: Plant divisions in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring or early fall, siting in slightly brighter light than the green species to keep the leaf variegation from fading.

directions: 'Variegata' pairs the stinking iris's legendary tolerance of dry, deep shade with leathery, evergreen leaves striped cream and green, giving year-round foliage interest well beyond the plain green species. Plant divisions in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring or early fall, siting it in slightly brighter light than the species requires to keep the variegation from fading back to green. The small mauve June flowers are followed in fall and winter by the same glistening orange-red seeds that split from fat pods, though this selection is typically a bit less vigorous and floriferous than its all-green counterpart.
sources: North Carolina State Extension -- Plants Database

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in late summer to early fall; this deep-rooted species resents disturbance once established.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in late summer to early fall, since this deep-rooted species resents being disturbed once established. A beardless European and western Asian native, spuria iris forms tall clumps of narrow, rush-like foliage topped in late spring to early summer, after bearded iris finish, by orchid-shaped blue-violet flowers marked with a yellow signal. It is the wild parent species behind decades of named spuria hybrids bred for the garden trade, and its extensive root system makes established clumps remarkably drought-tolerant despite needing consistent moisture through spring bloom.

common_name: Ledger's Variety Butterfly Iris (Hardy Fringed Iris Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; noted among butterfly iris selections for being hardier and more free-flowering than typical seed-grown plants.

directions: 'Ledger's Variety' is a long-grown selection of the butterfly iris, introduced to Western gardens in the nineteenth century and prized for being noticeably more free-flowering and slightly more cold-tolerant than typical seed-grown plants of the species. Plant divisions or rooted stolons in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring, where it will spread steadily to form broad, weed-suppressing colonies of flat evergreen fans. In mid-spring it produces abundant ruffled, orchid-like lavender-white flowers marked with orange-yellow crests, making it a reliable choice for naturalizing under high tree canopy where bearded iris would fail to bloom.

common_name: Variegata Japanese Roof Iris (Cream-Striped Roof Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions with the tops just below the soil surface in late summer to early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: 'Variegata' brings the same rare dry-shade tolerance as the green roof iris species to a plant grown chiefly for its cream-and-green striped, sword-shaped leaves, which provide season-long foliage interest whether or not it flowers. Plant rhizome divisions with the tops just below the soil surface in late summer to early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. It produces the same lilac-blue, dark-veined, crested flowers as the species in mid-spring, though typically in smaller numbers, since much of the plant's energy goes into maintaining its variegated foliage rather than bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in average to poor, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; tolerates extreme cold, drought, compaction, and mild salinity better than most garden iris.

directions: Native to the steppes, grasslands, and roadside ditches of northern China, Mongolia, and Central Asia, this tough, clump-forming species produces pale blue-violet to near-white flowers with darker veining above dense tufts of narrow, grass-like leaves in late spring. Plant divisions in average to poor, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun in fall, where it will tolerate extreme cold, prolonged drought, compacted soil, and even mild salinity that would kill most garden iris. Because it thrives on neglect, it is increasingly planted for erosion control and low-water roadside or prairie-style landscaping in harsh, cold-winter climates rather than as a typical border perennial.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed to the sun in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in late summer to early fall, exactly as for tall bearded iris.

directions: Native to the dry grasslands and rocky steppes of central and southeastern Europe through the Caucasus, this diminutive wild species is one of the principal ancestors of modern dwarf and intermediate bearded iris hybrids. Plant rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed to the sun in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in late summer to early fall, exactly as for tall bearded iris. It produces solitary, nearly stemless flowers in violet, yellow, or blue only a few inches above short blue-green foliage fans in the very earliest weeks of spring, often before daffodils finish, making it well suited to rock gardens and the front of a sunny, well-drained border where full-size bearded iris would be out of scale.
